title: Freundlich adsorption of acetic acid on charcoal: from a pH reading to the constant k
summary: One continuous run on a single dashboard: weigh and dissolve the acid, add charcoal, shake until a third of the molecules are stuck to the surface, measure the pH, turn it into the equilibrium concentration with Ka, plot the isotherm and finish with k - the answer appearing only when the run concludes.
subject: Chemistry
subtopics: Adsorption from solution onto a solid
Freundlich isotherm and its logarithmic form
Slope and intercept of the log-log plot
concepts: Adsorption is a surface process, so nothing leaves the flask - the adsorbate only changes address
A pH reading gives the hydrogen ion, not the weak acid that produced it
Ka is the conversion factor between [H+] and the concentration of an undissociated weak acid
The C in the Freundlich isotherm is the concentration left at equilibrium, never the initial one
Taking logarithms turns a power law into a straight line whose gradient is 1/n and whose intercept is log k
formulas: weak acid: Ka = [H+]^2 / C, so C = [H+]^2 / Ka
x = mass taken - mass left in solution

methods: Derived from first principles before any published solution was consulted: the mole calculation, the Ka inversion, the mass balance, the slope-to-n step and the final division were all fixed independently
The Ka route checked in both directions: forwards it gives C = 0.10 mol/L from pH 3.00, and substituting back, [H+] = sqrt(Ka x C) = 1.000e-3, reproducing the meter reading exactly

Conservation checked explicitly to machine precision: 0.30 g left in solution + 0.15 g adsorbed = 0.45 g weighed out, and the simulation enforces the same identity frame by frame while the flask is shaking
Two independent routes to k agree: dividing (x/m) by C gives 1.5, and the intercept of the log-log line gives log10 k = 0.176091, i.e. k = 1.500000
Units confirmed by dimensional analysis: (g/g) / (mol/L) = L/mol, which is the unit the question asks for - itself a check that x was correctly taken as a mass rather than a number of moles

The traps reproduced deliberately: using the initial 0.15 M gives exactly 1.0; treating pH 3 as the acid concentration gives an absurd 150; dividing by 50 instead of 0.050 L gives 0.00015; putting x in moles gives 0.025 L/g. None is 1.5

The intended approximation quantified rather than assumed: solving the weak-acid equilibrium exactly, without treating the acid left in solution as wholly undissociated, gives C = 0.1010 mol/L and k = 1.455 - a 3.0% shift. The question's round numbers are chosen so the standard approximation lands on a clean 1.5, which is the intended answer

Answer cross-checked afterwards against a published worked solution for this paper, which follows the same steps and reports the same intermediate values (1e-3 M, 0.10 M, 0.005 mol, 0.30 g, 0.15 g, n = 1) and the same answer, 1.5 L/mol. interactivity: One continuous experiment rather than separate exercises: seven steps, one primary action at a time, and the answer withheld until the run concludes

A single laboratory scene carries the whole run - digital balance, 50 mL measuring cylinder, conical flask on a shaker and a pH meter - changing state as each step is performed rather than being replaced by a new picture
A step rail across the top shows where the run has got to, with completed steps in green and the current one highlighted
The balance display counts up to 0.45 g and the acid then visibly disperses through the water as 45 dots, one per 0.01 g
Charcoal grains drawn as irregular porous particles; the flask rocks on the shaker and the liquid surface sways while the molecules move, collide with the grains and snap onto surface sites
A live instrument panel of thirteen gauges fills in as the run proceeds - measured quantities in blue, derived ones in green - so the dashboard shows exactly how much is known at any moment
Mass conservation is visible in the panel throughout the shake: the acid in solution falls and the acid adsorbed rises while the two always sum to the 0.45 g weighed out
The shake stops itself the moment adsorption reaches equilibrium and the run advances on its own
The pH probe descends down the neck of the flask and the meter settles from 7 down to 3.00 with a little noise before locking
The working appears one line at a time as the measurement behind it lands - nothing of the derivation is on the page before it has been earned
An animated mass-balance bar splits the 0.45 g into the 0.30 g still dissolved and the 0.15 g on the surface, with the arithmetic written underneath

The log-log plot places the measured point automatically, but the gradient is not handed over: it starts at 0.60 and the Calculate-k button stays locked until it is set to the value the question specifies

An animated slope triangle reports rise, run and rise/run so 1/n is read off rather than recalled, and the intercept is marked at log C = 0 and labelled log k as a second, independent route to the same number
The result box stays a placeholder until the final step, then reveals k = 1.5 L per mole

A concentration switch lets the student rerun the arithmetic with the initial 0.15 M and see the commonest wrong answer, 1.0, together with an explanation of which concentration the isotherm actually means
